articles.title: Republican wipeout: Trump created too many problems for himself and his party
articles.summary: What was expected to be a strong showing for the Democrats turned out to be a total wipeout of the Republican Party as we know it. The Democrats made massive gains in the House and the Senate. It was the kind of devastating outcome for Republicans that we haven’t seen in a while, the likes…
articles.body:
What was expected to be a strong showing for the Democrats turned out to be a total wipeout of the Republican Party as we know it. The Democrats made massive gains in the House and the Senate. It was the kind of devastating outcome for Republicans that we haven’t seen in a while, the likes of which it doesn’t just take a single election cycle to reverse.

Nearly every group that shifted toward Republicans in 2024 shifted back in 2026. So what happened?

It’s very simple: It was a cost-of-living election. Democrats were laser-focused on promising to address the cost of living crisis, whereas President Trump was laser-focused on … his ballroom. He was taking dinners with tech oligarchs. He was bragging about the stock market and oil profits — in other words, about how rich everyone except you is getting at the top.

Exit polls showed that the skyrocketing cost of living and government corruption were the top concerns of voters. Their lives have become unaffordable due to the exploding cost of housing, health care, education, insurance, utilities, and of course, groceries and gas.

Many voted for Trump in 2024 because they remembered the 2019 economy — when they had a little bit more money in their pockets at the end of the month.

That’s no longer so. Inflation has been outpacing wage growth for much of this year. So when Trump touted the “Golden Age of America” in rally after campaign rally, it wasn’t a rallying cry to the winners of a blazing hot economy — it was a finger in the eye of the losers in an economy whose vitality is based on tech speculation and the high gas prices that are killing consumers.

The constant reporting about extreme corruption at the highest levels of the Trump administration only added insult to injury. Former White House budget director and Trump chief of staff Mick Mulvaney appeared on my NewsNation show a few weeks ago. Reflecting on a poll that showed corruption as the top issue for 88 percent of voters, he remarked, “What people are telling the president is, ‘Look, we’re tired of you getting rich and us getting poor.'”

The Democrats’ analysis of their good fortune Tuesday night is spot on: Trump told people to vote like he was on the ballot, and they did.

But on the right, another singular explanation has emerged to explain the disaster we all witnessed unfold: the war in Iran, which was the third most important factor voters gave in exit polls explaining their vote.

Certainly, gas prices surged after the attack and still remain high. But as the exit polls show, the war in Iran was one of many things voters were upset about. And the thing that upset them about the war in Iran was not the attack itself, which was at least initially popular with Republican voters in many polls throughout March and even April. It was the fact that the war just kept going without any signs of a conclusion, becoming one more thing making their lives harder and more unaffordable.

A timeline of Trump’s approval ratings makes clear that although the war in Iran resulted in a steep dropoff, his approval really started to slip long before that — after the Liberation Day tariffs of April 2025. His approval rating has never recovered from that.

I believe that Trump and his party could have survived any one of these problems, but not all three. If the cost of housing and health care and groceries were coming down, a dollar more per gallon at the pump would have been more tolerable. If Trump had not spent so much time talking up the ballroom and other expensive vanity projects, voters might have had more patience with the tariffs.

If voters felt like they were making money, they might have minded less that everyone in the president’s orbit seems to be making billions off the presidency, some of them through dodgy cryptocurrency schemes.

It was everything together that revealed a presidency simply unable to focus on the main promises of his campaign in 2024. Those promises were fourfold: Radically reduce immigration; bring costs down and get money back in the pockets of working Americans; drain the swamp; and no new wars. He succeeded at only one, failing rather ostentatiously at all the others.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “ Batya !” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the nation’s fastest-growing cable news network and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The buzz about the presidential election is already under way - here's what we learned this week.
articles.body:
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.

Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro , swept aside his Republican challenger.

Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.

On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.

Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure

Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.

That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .

"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.

Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.

Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.

In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz , who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.

"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis , who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.

White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future

Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.

Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.

El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.

His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.

This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.

Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.

Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.

Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned

Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.

Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.

Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".

That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.

"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.

"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.

"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: DOJ shake-up continues with head of national security division, US attorney in Miami resigning
articles.summary: John Eisenberg and Miami U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones are leaving the Justice Department, one day after Harmeet Dhillon announced her departure.
articles.body: John Eisenberg, the head of the National Security Division at the Department of Justice, is stepping down from his post, becoming the third senior DOJ official to resign since the midterm elections. Shortly after Fox News learned of Eisenberg's resignation, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced it on social media. "He has served with distinction, strengthening our nation’s ability to address threats, both foreign and domestic," Blanche said. "Under his leadership, the Division advanced President Trump’s mission to make America safe by prosecuting terrorists and working with our law enforcement partners to disrupt planned attacks on the American people." This was Eisenberg's second stint serving under President Donald Trump. In Trump's first term, Eisenberg was an assistant and deputy counsel to the president, as well as a legal advisor to the National Security Council, which advises presidents on foreign policy matters. DOJ CIVIL RIGHTS CHIEF HARMEET DHILLON RESIGNS, SAYS WHITE HOUSE ASKED HER TO WAIT UNTIL AFTER MIDTERMS Less than an hour before Eisenberg's departure was made public, Blanche announced the resignation of Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. Attorney for Florida's Southern District. Quiñones was perhaps best known for securing an indictment against Raúl Castro, the former president of Cuba who took over after his brother Fidel Castro's nearly 50-year reign. Raúl Castro, now 95, was indicted for his alleged role in the 1996 shoot-down of two unarmed civilian aircraft operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based humanitarian group that searched the Florida Straits for Cuban migrants in distress. The four U.S. nationals aboard the two planes were killed. "We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime," Blanche said. "Jason has served the Department multiple times over his distinguished career, and we thank him for his service to this country." DOJ LAUNCHES CRIMINAL PROBE INTO SUPREME COURT LEAK THAT EXPOSED RULING OVERTURNING ROE V WADE The departure of Eisenberg and Quiñones came just a day after Harmeet Dhillon, who headed up the DOJ's Civil Rights Division, announced she'd be leaving as well. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Dhillon said she attempted to resign three weeks ago but was asked by White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles to stay until after the midterms. Dhillon moved to Washington following the deaths of her husband and father to "serve my country," but after roughly two years in the administration, she said it was time for her to leave. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Dhillon shifted her office's priorities toward issues including DEI and race-conscious policies, religious discrimination, transgender participation in women's sports, Second Amendment rights and election integrity. In the lead-up to the midterms, Dhillon defended the Trump administration's investigation into noncitizen voters. She was also in charge of the DOJ's effort to send more than 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states.

articles.title: ‘Voter apathy’ toward Hyde-Smith could be factor in Mississippi Senate race: Professor
articles.summary: A Mississippi political science professor said voters seemed to be “really enthusiastic” about Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, but when it comes to his opponent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), “there was a lot of voter apathy.” “Colom’s a really high-quality candidate,” Aaron Hitefield, assistant professor in the Mississippi State University Department of Political Science and…
articles.body:
A Mississippi political science professor said voters seemed to be “really enthusiastic” about Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, but when it comes to his opponent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R), “there was a lot of voter apathy.”

“Colom’s a really high-quality candidate,” Aaron Hitefield, assistant professor in the Mississippi State University Department of Political Science and Public Administration, said during an appearance on NewsNation.

“Voters seemed really enthusiastic about him … when you compare that to Cindy Hyde-Smith, the current incumbent, there was a lot of voter apathy,” Hitefield added. “I think you see that in the results currently.”

The Senate race in the historically red-leaning state remains uncalled as Colom maintains a lead of a little more than 2,000 votes, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ . In the neck and neck battle for a seat in the U.S. Senate, the Democrat is leading by just 0.2 percentage points.

Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst told the press Thursday that if “the laws are followed and the voters spoke, that is it and Mississippi Republicans will accept that .”

“There is no election denying going on here,” he said.

The ballots are still being received in the Magnolia State, which allows mail ballots to be counted and received up to five business days after the election as long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

Attorneys for Hyde-Smith recently demanded in a letter sent to the election commissioners in all 82 Mississippi counties that election officials separate the affidavit ballots, document their disposition and preserve “all associated materials.”

An attorney for Colom , in a letter sent to county election commissioners Thursday, said the Republicans’ demands “have no basis in Mississippi law.”

“If you depart from ordinary election procedures as you have been asked to do, you will violate Mississippi voters’ rights and Mississippi election law,” the lawyer wrote in the letter.

By current tally, the Democrats will hold 54 Senate seats and, with Mississippi and Alaska still undecided, that number could grow to 56.

articles.title: Democrats win big after Trump alienates voters
articles.summary: Donald Trump’s rhetoric and policy failures contributed to significant losses for Republicans in congressional elections, even as Democrats secured victories across several key states.
articles.body:
President Trump told Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. They did. And now a lot of Republicans probably wish the president had never opened his mouth.

It wasn’t a blue wave — it was a blue earthquake, as the New York Times put it . It’s not easy to lose both houses of Congress — but thanks to the president, Republicans managed to do just that.

Two years ago Trump told voters that when he’s elected president, inflation would come down. It’s higher today than when Joe Biden left office. He promised lower food prices. Anybody who’s been to a supermarket lately knows how that worked out. He said the war with Iran would last a few weeks. Wrong again.

A recent NBC News poll finds that 71 percent of Americans think we’re on the wrong track . You’d think a number like that might have persuaded the president to spend the closing days of the campaign talking about grocery bills.

But Trump had a few other things on his mind. He spoke about his fascination with the rear ends of a Republican senator and singer Nicki Minaj .

The day before Election Day, in his final public speech, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and spoke for more than 20 minutes about gravel, new grass, pipes and algae.

A week earlier he told a rally that “ Norway sucks ” because the folks there who hand out the Nobel Peace Prize neglected to give him one.

He called Bill Maher “ a complete and total loser ” because Maher apparently didn’t give the president the respect he thinks he deserves.

Imagine being a Republican candidate in a close race, hoping the president might say a few words about the cost of living, but instead you get his musings about algae, Norway, Bill Maher and rear ends.

Make no mistake, Republicans got what they deserved. For two years they said virtually nothing about tariffs or the war or those inexcusable pardons on his first day in office of the rioters at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — or anything else Trump said or did that hurt the party. Not in public, anyway. In private they knew what everybody else knew — that the president was in way over his head … on the war, on inflation, on affordability, which he recklessly called a “hoax.”

He never told the voters that he understood their pain. He couldn’t. Because he has no empathy.

His Republican allies may think they were being loyal to their leader, but it was shameless cowardice dressed up as loyalty. Sycophancy comes with a price — a price Republicans are now paying.

In the world of politics, there is nothing especially remarkable about a president hurting his enemies. It takes a special talent to do this much damage to your friends.

But in spite of everything, Trump did have a legitimate case to make against the Democrats. When he told voters that the party’s left wing wanted to usher in a socialist America, he could point to progressives whose wish-list includes a national wealth tax, Medicare for all, abolishment of ICE, abandonment of Israel — and that’s for openers. Some progressives would go further and move for a federal takeover of some corporations. The Democratic Socialists of America want to defund the police and shut down prisons . They have no use for capitalism and aren’t afraid to say so.

And yet, in spite of all that, the Democrats won, because it wasn’t only Trump’s policies that voters rejected — it was Trump himself. They rejected his vulgarity, his out-of-control narcissism, his unlimited appetite for vengeance.

And the worst of Trump rubbed off on the president’s allies, who somehow figured that nastiness might be the path to victory.

In Kansas, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R) accused his Democratic opponent of “probably grooming” children . Marshall lost.

In Texas, Republicans insinuated that Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is gay. Talarico won.

And President Trump called Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “ vicious, violent jihadist .” El-Sayed won.

So did Democratic Senate candidates in Maine, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina — and before it’s over, maybe a few more states.

As impressive as the Democratic victory was, it was hardly a mandate for them to do a lot of things nobody voted for. Do Americans really want Trump impeached for a third time? Progressives might, but they don’t represent Middle America. Do Americans really want non-stop investigations of Trump and anybody that got close to him during the past two years? Do they want the socialist wing of the party to run roughshod over more moderate Democrats?

If Democrats don’t bring down prices and give Americans hope that we’re heading in the right direction, in two years they may very well be where Republicans are now: devastated and disheartened, on the outside looking in.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page .

articles.title: Blue wave battered GOP strongholds across America, but one red state held the line
articles.summary: South Dakota's GOP held firm as Dan Ahler's moderate Democrat strategy fell flat, even as similar campaigns slashed Republican margins elsewhere.
articles.body: On a night when Democrats made major gains across the country, South Dakota emerged as one of the few Republican strongholds where the GOP largely held its ground — even as Democrats made inroads around Sioux Falls. Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden won roughly 63.5% of the vote Tuesday, nearly matching President Donald Trump's 63.4% performance in 2024. Republicans also swept the state's other statewide races and maintained overwhelming control of the legislature, despite Democrats picking up four seats. Rhoden's victory came against Democrat Dan Ahlers, who described himself as a "conservative Democrat" and campaigned on affordability, rural healthcare, education and other kitchen table issues. But his moderate pitch did little to narrow the GOP's commanding statewide advantage, with Ahlers finishing at just 36.5% of the vote. South Dakota's results stood in contrast to several other deeply Republican states where the GOP maintained control but saw its margins shrink considerably. In Idaho and Wyoming, Republican gubernatorial candidates won comfortably but finished with smaller shares of the vote than President Donald Trump secured in 2024. South Dakota's gubernatorial result, by comparison, remained virtually unchanged. DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED David Jolly, the Democratic nominee in Florida, ran a campaign with similar themes to Ahlers' — pointing to the fact that he used to be a Republican and, like Ahlers, prioritized affordability and healthcare while on the campaign trail. Jolly cut the GOP’s vote share to just 50%, roughly six points below the party’s 2024 presidential performance. Tennessee's Democratic gubernatorial nominee inflicted a similarly sharp cut on Republicans' margins by employing a similar strategy. Even down the ballot, South Dakota Republicans largely held their ground, though Democrats managed to flip four legislative seats in the Sioux Falls area, marking their first legislative gains in the state since 2008. The losses were concentrated around the state's largest city, where a growing population and a less conservative political landscape have created more opportunities for Democrats, according to University of South Dakota political scientist Julia Hellwege. Opposition to large data-center projects also resonated with some voters in the area, according to a local Democratic official. "South Dakota Republicans did well because we took on the issues that mattered to the people of our state and delivered real results for them," South Dakota's Republican House speaker, Jon Hansen, told Fox News Digital. "The bottom line is that we ran on tackling the issues that mattered to people, and then we delivered real results for the people on those issues. Not just talk, not just excuses, but real solutions. It’s what our people deserve, and it’s what we delivered for them." FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS Hansen pointed to property tax cuts enacted by the legislature, regulations aimed at preventing utility costs from rising amid data center build-outs, curbing corporate eminent domain and balancing the state's budget, among other efforts, as crucial in the South Dakota GOP's success on Tuesday night. South Dakota’s unemployment rate has been hovering around 2% since last September, roughly half the rate of the United States at large. Average wages also increased by about 4% in the state over the course of 2025. All of this occurred as South Dakota remained one of the most affordable states in the country, though rising rent costs outpaced wage growth in 2025, according to data collected by Realtor.com. At the federal level, Republican Sen. Mike Rounds cruised to victory with 60.5% of the vote, though the GOP wasn't entirely immune to the national shift. South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley won the state's at-large congressional seat with roughly 64% of the vote, down from the 72% fellow Republican Dusty Johnson secured in 2024. South Dakota's relatively modest legislative losses stood in sharp contrast to other Republican strongholds. In Texas, Democrats flipped 21 GOP-held state House seats, while Republicans in New Hampshire were on track to fall from the 222 House seats they won in 2024 to just 107. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Republicans in Arizona, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Georgia, North Carolina and Michigan all lost control of at least one chamber of their state legislatures on Tuesday night. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Those Republicans who lost on Nov. 3 did so because their actions (or inaction) didn’t match their promises to voters. We didn’t have that problem in South Dakota under our leadership," South Dakota's GOP House Majority Leader, Rep. Scott Odenbach, told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Sununu blames Trump for GOP midterm shellacking
articles.summary: Senate Republican candidate John Sununu says President Trump deserves much of the blame for Republicans’ blowout losses in Tuesday’s election, which will give Democrats their biggest Senate and House majorities in years. Sununu in an interview with SiriusXM’s “The John Kasich Show” said Trump’s inability to end the months-long conflict with Iran and his failure…
articles.body:
Senate Republican candidate John Sununu says President Trump deserves much of the blame for Republicans’ blowout losses in Tuesday’s election, which will give Democrats their biggest Senate and House majorities in years.

Sununu in an interview with SiriusXM’s “The John Kasich Show” said Trump’s inability to end the months-long conflict with Iran and his failure to “drain the swamp” as he pledged to do in the 2024 campaign cost Republican candidates dearly.

“Now it seems like he or his family is on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” Sununu said. “Those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can’t vote for a Republican while he’s still in office.'”

Sununu lost the New Hampshire Senate race to Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) by 13 percentage points despite Republican hopes that they had a good chance of stealing the Democratic-held seat.

Sununu represented New Hampshire in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, when he was defeated by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.)

Trump, however, has blamed GOP candidates for not doing a good enough job of promoting themselves and has argued that he would have carried many of them to victory if he were on the ballot as he was two years ago.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump posted on Truth Social on Tuesday night as the election returns showed a blue wave sweeping across the country.

Vice President Vance on Wednesday cited the war with Iran as the biggest reason why Republicans fared so poorly in this year’s midterm election.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a social media post.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance argued.

“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” he said.

But some Republican strategists are acknowledging privately that Democrats’ attacks on Trump’s family business dealings and other allegations of corruption in the Trump administration also moved voters.

Sununu told “The John Kasich Show” that future Republican presidential aspirants such as Vance will suffer political fallout after Republicans’ disastrous showing in the midterms.

“The closer you are to the president, the worse a night it was for you as a potential presidential candidate,” he said.

Sununu predicted that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) would explore a presidential run in the next election cycle to boost her political brand.

“Some people run for president because they really think they can win and that they’ll be a great leader and an important leader for the country. Some people run for president because it’s good for their business model,” he said.

“And I put AOC in the latter category. So, will she test the waters and go through the kabuki? One hundred percent. Because her business model is built around followers and attention,” he added.

articles.title: Don Jr. Knifes His Dad With Brutal Election Reality Check
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s eldest son has been surprisingly candid in calling out why his father’s candidates got “smoked” in the midterms. Donald Trump Jr. ad...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's eldest son has been surprisingly candid in calling out why his father's candidates got "smoked" in the midterms.

Donald Trump Jr. admits MAGA voters turned on Republicans because his dad launched a war with Iran after promising on the campaign trail that a vote for him was a vote for no new wars.

"I've seen a few talking heads—guys like, you know, Mark Thiessen out there trying to claim that the Iran war had nothing to do with Republicans losing, right? There's no downside to the Iran War," Don Jr. said on his Triggered podcast. "Disgusting, actually."

He continued, "Whether you think it was the right decision or not, the Iran War is largely what shifted voter sentiment and caused this wave, right? It jacked up the price of gas. That's the thing that people feel most immediately in their pockets, and it changed their minds."

The younger Trump, 48, suggested that voters do not care whether the war is the right thing to do or not—they care that they did not get what they voted for.

"We also campaigned on not getting into these things, and we don't have to debate whether it was the right thing or the wrong thing," Don Jr. said. "I don't have any of the details. I'm not privy to any of that in terms of the intelligence. But it was definitely something after Afghanistan and Iraq that we probably didn't want to be into."

He added, "Even though I don't believe this is going to be one of those forever wars, and I bring this up mainly just to say that we're only going to rebuild if we're actually honest about what happened. It's frankly vital that the Republican Party understand that voters aren't just going to give them the benefit of the doubt, especially in a midterm when my father himself isn't on the ballot."

Don Jr. called Tuesday's results a "blue tsunami" and a "wake-up call." To swing the pendulum back for Republicans in two years, he says the party has to be honest with how they got here. He has endorsed Vice President JD Vance's Election Day postmortem, which said it was war with Iran that cost Republicans all-important Senate seats in typically ruby-red states like South Carolina, Kansas, and Iowa.

"The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump-Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in '26," Don Jr. said. "Honestly, no excuses here. A lot of our voters showed up, but we lost a lot of them, too."

Don Jr. said Trump voters do not owe MAGA anything if they are not pleased with the results.

"Was every voter thrilled with how enforcement has been handled as it relates to immigration? No, and I'm not going to sit here and pretend otherwise," Don Jr. said. "The exit polls say 57 percent thought it went too far, but here's the thing: we really need to understand these voters don't owe us anything. They can make up their own minds. A lot of them were Democrats 10 years ago. A lot of them never voted before 2016. They didn't sign up for a party. They signed up for Trump and the MAGA movement."

articles.title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
articles.summary: Jim Messina tells the BBC that after Democrats' midterm victories he's talked to "over two dozen campaigns", with some already hiring staff.
articles.body:
More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.

"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.

He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.

He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"

Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.

"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.

"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."

Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".

"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.

Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.

"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.

Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".

The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

articles.title: Paraguay resumes Pena impeachment proceedings as financial crisis deepens
articles.summary: Political turmoil comes after a digital bank’s failure has left half the population without access to their accounts.
articles.body:
Lawmakers in Paraguay have resumed impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Pena, a day after he resigned amid links to the country’s worst financial crisis in decades.

The Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove the conservative economist from office.

Politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president on Thursday, despite his resignation. Pena, who was elected in 2023, has requested a 72-hour extension to prepare his defence before the Senate.

The proceedings follow a vote in Paraguay’s lower house of Congress, where lawmakers overwhelmingly approved impeachment charges against Pena in a 78-0 vote.

The political turmoil surrounding the country’s president follows Paraguay’s central bank’s intervention earlier this week at Ueno Bank, one of the country’s fastest-growing digital lenders, citing breaches of minimum solvency requirements.

Pena previously held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, until last year, when he claims he sold his shares. Paraguayan lawmakers have accused the president of a conflict of interest and questioned whether authorities failed to act on warnings about the lender’s financial position.

The collapse of Ueno, which held $850m in public funds, has left more than half of Paraguay’s population without access to their accounts, drawing intense scrutiny over the government’s relationship with the bank and financial regulators’ effectiveness.

“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds — as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans — be protected,” Pena said in a Thursday video address where he apologised for failing to prevent the crisis.

The crisis has also prompted the resignation of Paraguay’s central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, and arrest warrants for eight Ueno executives, who later turned themselves in.

Paraguay’s attorney general has ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, including its regulatory oversight and the placement of public funds in the institution.

If Pena is convicted in an impeachment trial, he would lose the lifetime Senate seat and associated legal protections ordinarily granted to former Paraguayan presidents.

articles.title: Democrat who toppled GOP incumbent will head to court on felony charge just days after election upset
articles.summary: Democrat Lakesha Womack, who defeated Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina, reportedly faces felony charges over an unreturned rental car.
articles.body: Just one week after pulling off a surprise victory over incumbent Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District race, Democrat LaKesha Womack is set to appear in court on a pending felony charge. Womack secured 51.1% of the vote in the House race, while Moore received 48.9%, according to election results reported by The Associated Press. The Mecklenburg County Sheriff’s Office previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Womack had been served a criminal summons on Oct. 11 by a deputy with the Polk County Sheriff’s Office on a pending felony charge alleging she failed to return a rental vehicle valued at $20,000 in 2019. The criminal summons was issued in January 2020 but not served until 2026, according to WBTV. Womack is set to appear in court on Nov. 10, The New York Post reported Thursday. REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Womack previously acknowledged failing to return the rental car on time, saying she was experiencing homelessness at the time and was unaware that a criminal case had been filed against her. "This historic victory is bigger than me. It is a testament to the power of ordinary people who believe that their voices matter and that leadership should be rooted in service, accountability, and opportunity for all," Womack told Fox News Digital in a statement on Friday. "As a Black woman, a single mother, an entrepreneur, and someone who has spent more than two decades helping communities grow, I understand both the challenges people face and the possibilities we can create together." DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN "We didn't just make history in North Carolina's 14th Congressional District; we opened the door for a new generation of leaders who listen, learn, and lead for the people," she continued. When asked about facing the felony charge on Friday, Womack declined to comment to Fox News Digital. Under North Carolina law, the charge is a Class H felony that can carry a prison sentence exceeding two years, depending on the defendant's criminal history and other sentencing factors. Under House rules, members formally charged with a felony punishable by two or more years in prison are expected to step aside from committee assignments and party leadership positions while the charges remain pending, a provision that could become relevant to Womack once she takes office in January. "My opponent needs to explain these pending felony charges to the voters of North Carolina District 14," Moore wrote in an Oct. 28 post on X. "With a court date literally the week after the election this is a big deal."

articles.title: Russia secretly bolstered Iran's missile arsenal before war with US, records uncover
articles.summary: Internal Russian defense documents reveal a contract for 90 precision-guided missile launchers destined for Iran, detailing Moscow's military support.
articles.body: Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S. A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted. President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all." IRAN TAPS FINANCIAL LIFELINE, RUSSIAN ARMS AS TRUMP ESCALATES 'CRUSHING' ECONOMIC WARFARE Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025. Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation. The K-10 designation can also be traced to Russian military hardware that ultimately reached Iran. An internal Russian production schedule listed six Yak-130 aircraft for a consignee identified as K-10. Iranian state media later showed the aircraft entering service in September 2023, and Dallas Analytics said the tail number of one Iranian Yak-130 matched the number listed for K-10 in the Russian factory records. The APU-L launchers are designed to carry Russia's LMUR, a precision-guided missile also known as Product 305 or the Kh-39. The roughly 230-pound missile carries a 55-pound warhead and can be guided in flight by an operator using an electro-optical seeker and two-way radio link. FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE Iran had already publicly announced plans to acquire Russian Mi-28 attack helicopters, one of the platforms capable of carrying the weapon. The first export-variant Mi-28NE helicopters were photographed in Iran in January 2026. The paperwork also shows involvement by Russia's Defense Ministry. A May 2024 letter accompanying the K-10 production schedule was co-signed by the head of the ministry's 123rd Military Representation. The documents do not establish whether the completed launchers ultimately reached Iran, though Dallas Analytics told Fox News Digital the contract itself is "a very strong proof" of the transfer. SATELLITE IMAGES MAY HAVE TIPPED OFF IRAN BEFORE US BASE ATTACK, TOP REPUBLICAN WARNS The findings add new detail to a military relationship the Trump administration has repeatedly played down during the war. U.S. intelligence has assessed that Russia provided Iran with information on the location of American military assets and, more recently, satellite imagery and weapons components, according to reports. But administration officials have said that support has not materially affected the U.S. campaign. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russian assistance was not impeding U.S. military operations, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said the U.S. was tracking Moscow's support and accounting for it in its battle plans. The Trump administration has separately sought to disrupt Iran's foreign weapons procurement as Tehran works to rebuild its military capabilities. The Treasury Department has targeted networks it says helped Iran seek weapons and components abroad, including efforts to acquire Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Just this week, the State Department sanctioned a Russia-based individual it said was involved in efforts to help Iran procure Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS. Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, State Department and Department of War for comment.

articles.title: Andrews says she won’t be focused on ‘retribution tour’
articles.summary: South Carolina’s newly elected senator, Annie Andrews (D), said her focus will be on “delivering results” and not a “retribution tour” following her victory in the midterm elections. In the historically red state of South Carolina, Andrews won a competitive Senate race against Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who was picked to succeed her late…
articles.body:
South Carolina’s newly elected senator, Annie Andrews (D), said her focus will be on “delivering results” and not a “retribution tour” following her victory in the midterm elections.

In the historically red state of South Carolina, Andrews won a competitive Senate race against Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.), who was picked to succeed her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Andrews won by more than 4 percentage points and more tahn 90,000 votes, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill. The forecaster narrowly favored Darline Graham ahead of the elections.

“Fighting the administration is not going to lower gas prices and grocery prices. It’s not going to solve the problems that I heard about for the past eighteen months,” Andrews told Fox News during an interview . “So I’m going to be laser-focused on delivering results and not, you know, a retribution tour, because that’s what the people of South Carolina are expecting from me.”

Andrews also said she is willing to work with President Trump “to secure the border, to stop these Medicaid cuts” and to “find a way out of this war.”

“I’m going to walk up to the halls of Congress and do my best to solve as many problems as I can for the people of South Carolina,” she added.

Andrews, a pediatrician, launched her bid to run for a seat in the U.S. Senate last year. She previously ran for office in 2022 against Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), losing by around 14 points. Four years later, she won her Senate bid, becoming the first Democrat to hold a Senate seat from the state in decades.

Andrews’s win is consistent with the Democrats’ nationwide victory in the midterm elections this November, where the party took control of both the Senate and the House. Democrats secured big wins in battleground states, flipping GOP-held seats in places like Texas, Maine, Iowa, Ohio and Michigan.

articles.title: AI companies’ deceptive election ads show why Congress must scrutinize super PACs
articles.summary: Public Citizen and Issue One advocates for the Sunlight on SuperPACs Act to require campaign ads to disclose their top three donors, following reports that the AI industry used shell groups to hide over $69 million in midterms spending.
articles.body:
In many of the hottest races in this year’s midterm elections, data centers and artificial intelligence companies were effectively on the ballot. The AI industry knew how unpopular they have become, with voters across the political spectrum furious at them. So, how then could an unpopular industry pour more than $69 million into campaign ads to boost AI-friendly politicians without having their ads backfire when angry voters find out who’s behind them? Simple: Hide who really paid for the ads behind fake names.

This was perfectly legal — and perfectly outrageous.

Following in the footsteps of a slew of other unpopular corporate interests and billionaires before them who knew their names were toxic with voters, the AI industry’s super PAC ads hid their sponsorship behind generically named shell groups like “Defending Our Values,” “Think Big,” “American Mission,” and “Jobs and Democracy.” Almost none of the AI industry’s super PAC ads mentioned data centers or AI at all.

This is not something that favored one side or another; it’s a bipartisan problem. An AI super PAC ad for a Republican candidate featured the phrase “CHAMPION AMERICAN INNOVATION” as he shook hands with firefighters, with no mention of data centers or AI. Another AI super PAC ad for a Democrat running for a House seat praised the candidate as committed to reducing gun violence and supporting law enforcement — no mention of AI. The ads were labeled as paid for by a generically named group, not “paid for by AI companies.”

Voters deserve to know who’s really paying for the ads they see so they can make informed decisions at the ballot box. Access to actionable information is at the heart of a healthy democracy — and the very essence of what the First Amendment was designed to protect.

Congress must close this deceptive super PAC ad loophole before the 2028 elections. The good news is that a recently introduced bill would do exactly that. Inspired by successful voter-approved campaign disclosure laws in Alaska, Arizona and California that passed with cross-partisan support, the Sunlight on SuperPACs Act recently introduced by Reps. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) and Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.) would enact a simple labeling law requiring all super PAC-funded campaign ads to include the names of their top three donors and how much they donated.

In the case of the AI-funded super PAC ads, they could still use their shell committees to pay for them, but they would have to let voters know that the top funders of the shell committees are AI companies, executives or billionaires. That would give voters the real-time information they need to be able to evaluate the credibility of the ads by seeing who’s paying for them when they’re seeing the ads. Voters are smart but can’t make informed decisions without information.

Courts have already heard multiple corporate-funded challenges to similar state disclosure laws and upheld them all. While we strongly believe that the Supreme Court in Citizens United v. FEC was deeply mistaken in concluding that the First Amendment required allowing corporations to spend unlimited sums to influence elections, the court did unequivocally affirm the constitutionality of campaign disclosure laws.

The Supreme Court has long recognized as consistent with the First Amendment the people’s “informational interest” in requiring election campaigns to provide voters with information about the funders of election ads. Because donor transparency “enables the electorate to make informed decisions and give proper weight to different speakers and messages,” the court has consistently upheld disclosure laws. We are confident it would uphold a super PAC funders labeling law too.

Putting a true source funding label at the bottom of super PAC ads would not address the obscene amount of money being spent on American politics today or limit the questionable claims corporations and billionaires make in their campaign ads. But the Sunlight on SuperPACs Actwill empower voters to be informed about who’s behind the ads they see. Then voters can evaluate the merits of the ads for themselves. We urge the next Congress to give voters that information and shine sunlight on super PACs.

Jon Golinger is the democracy advocate for Public Citizen . Michael Beckel is Money in Politics Reform director for Issue One .

articles.title: ‘A Republican will never sniff the White House ever again’ if Texas stays blue: Jesse Watters
articles.summary: Fox News anchor Jesse Watters warned that if Republicans cannot return to power in Texas, the GOP may never win the presidency again. Watters said during his show Thursday night that Democrats’ sweeping wins in the midterm elections could be a death knell for Republicans’ chances of winning future presidential elections. Democrats won all statewide…
articles.body:
Fox News anchor Jesse Watters warned that if Republicans cannot return to power in Texas, the GOP may never win the presidency again.

Watters said during his show Thursday night that Democrats’ sweeping wins in the midterm elections could be a death knell for Republicans’ chances of winning future presidential elections.

Democrats won all statewide elections on the ballot Tuesday, leaving Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) as the only remaining GOP statewide official in the Lone Star State.

“They seize Texas and are on pace for the biggest midterm landslide since Watergate,” Watters said. “Now, if Texas stays blue, a Republican will never sniff the White House ever again.”

The Fox News personality said Republicans had two years to target Democratic opponents without many clear successes, warning that Democrats won’t “take it easy” on the GOP.

“They want it extinguished. They’re already talking about abolishing the Electoral College, impeaching the president, and executing Elon Musk. Democrat governors now control a majority of states where most of the population lives,” Watters added.

No Democratic elected official has called for the execution of Musk.

Watters said Democrats’ near-win among white voters this cycle reinforced the Republican struggle. After showing a video of a Texas Democratic lawmaker talking about minority races joining to form a majority voting bloc in America, Watters said after Tuesday — that could work.

“They’re talking about uniting the minority races against whites. Texas Democrat politicians are declaring a political race war. And they could win, because Republicans nearly lost the white vote Tuesday,” he said.

“Democrats are on the cusp of winning a majority of whites, Blacks and Hispanics. Open borders is suicide. The Democrats are about to win a Senate seat in Mississippi. Black guy. That’s like Republicans winning Hawaii,” Watters continued.

The Fox News host said “a lot” of the blame for the midterm losses can also be pinned on the candidates, specifically Ken Paxton (R) in Texas and Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). He said the GOP’s loss Tuesday was not a usual midterm correction.

“This wasn’t your standard midterm thumping,” Watters said. “When [former President] Obama got blown out in 2010 and 2014, those races were close. And he didn’t almost lose the Black vote like Republicans almost lost the white vote.”

articles.title: Dems pivot from ‘affordability’ pitch to DHS probe threats after midterm wins
articles.summary: Robert Garcia and other Democrats campaigned on affordability but pivoted to subpoenas and Trump investigations after winning, Fox News Digital found.
articles.body: Several prominent Democrats who ran on an "affordability" message were largely silent when pressed by Fox News Digital on their sudden pivot to foreshadowing investigations into the Trump administration, including in many cases its immigration enforcement efforts. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is poised to lead the House Oversight Committee, responded to Democrats' win Tuesday with a statement: "Lawyer Up", despite having pledged to prioritize household costs alongside government accountability. Garcia told CNN before the election that "Democratic priorities" would be lowering the cost of "gas, groceries, the mortgage, the rent," alongside combating government corruption. PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP In response to a request for comment, a representative for Garcia shared a tweet he posted Wednesday, after his Tuesday "lawyer up" warning, that referenced affordability: "People can’t afford gas, groceries, and rent because Donald Trump and his family are ripping off the American people and enriching themselves. Taking on corruption is about making life more affordable for working families," Garcia said in the tweet. Before the election, "Squad" Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., wrote in a PBS-Chicago voters guide that there is "no question that the rising cost of living is the number one issue" for a "working people’s agenda." After the election, however, her tone appeared to change: "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up? Clear your schedule," Ramirez said. Several respondents pushed back, including one of her stated targets, former Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino. "Honey, slow your totalitarian roll," Bovino responded on X. "Citizens don’t answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that." Bovino went on to suggest Ramirez instead relax with a bottle of whiskey from a brand the former immigration official launched upon retirement. Other respondents also pointed out that Ramirez’ post-election missive didn’t mention her affordability priority: SCHUMER PREACHES AFFORDABILITY IN DEM MIDTERM PITCH WHILE SABOTAGING GOP FIXES FOR SOARING COSTS "Notice nothing about how she is going to help her constituents but ‘get Trump’," said one. "So, you guys never really gave a s--- about affordability," added former Energy Department staffer Matt van Swol. Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., who now represents the longtime Republican-held seat of former Rep. Rodney Frelinghuysen, made both affordability and immigration policy part of her campaign message. "We’re going to toss out subpoenas like Mardi Gras beads," Mejia’s first X post Wednesday read. Rep. Tony Wied, R-Wis., responded it showed Democrats "have no plans to make life better for you," eliciting a response from Mejia in which she dubbed him "Mr. Weird" and only then mentioned an "economy that works for" Americans. In April, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., released a lengthy statement announcing a "New Affordability Agenda" and highlighting her role on the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ "Lowering Costs Task Force." On Election Night, Ansari posted: "Thank you Mr. President. Our thank-you will come in January with subpoenas." An ensuing tweet called for the impeachment of War Secretary Pete Hegseth. On Wednesday, Ansari ultimately posted a policy-related pledge to curtail AI. Sen. Edward Markey, D-Mass., stated during the midterms that his priorities were "groceries, gas prices energy costs" and the like. However, his post-election missive remarking on how many "new forests" will need planting for "all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing," instead signaled a priority to investigate tech executives like Elon Musk. "Affordability," quipped former Virginia Del. Nick Freitas, R-Culpeper, in a reply. Ramirez, Mejia, Markey and Ansari did not respond to requests for comment on their apparent pivots. Garcia’s representative responded by providing his subsequent post on affordability. Both Garcia and Ramirez had previously identified government accountability and immigration oversight, respectively, as priorities, but their immediate post-election statements emphasized investigations rather than the affordability measures they had highlighted on the campaign trail. DHS appeared to take the newfound priority in stride in comments to Fox News Digital. "It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing," said DHS’ top attorney James Percival. "Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland," the counsel said. A Justice Department spokesperson echoed Percival, saying the agency is "not afraid of threats from Democrats" and assured its staff has followed the law. "It is no surprise that rather than focus on bringing down costs for Americans, Democrats in Congress are picking up where their weaponization efforts left off when they were last in power," the spokesperson said. Meanwhile, the White House told Fox News Digital that Trump remains willing to work with Democrats on issues they can collaborate on to help "hardworking Americans." "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. Immigration hawks signaled preparations for what Democrats foreshadowed. The Mass Deportation Coalition, whose leaders have been critical of Biden-era open-border policies and have asserted that the Trump administration has not done enough on the issue in some areas, told Fox News Digital they are prepared to defend officials amid the onslaught. "We know what’s coming," said Mass Deportation Coalition leader Mike Howell. "A lot of people are going to be cashing-out and charging patriots expensive legal fees to the most vulnerable." "We have been through this before and are ready to sacrifice for the patriots who are targeted by weaponized harassment." Former House Oversight Committee counsel and immigration judge Andrew Arthur said Congress has the prerogative to investigate DHS’ work but added that it may not be what Americans are looking for as a priority. Citing Ramirez’ mention of Border Czar Tom Homan, Arthur noted that the onetime Obama official long held "positive" ratings from Republicans and Democrats. "He was commonly viewed as the guy who came in and cleaned things up after Noem left, got things a little bit better. So that's probably not going to be a terribly popular thing," he said. "This isn't really affordability but anything that shows waste in government technically goes to affordability and it all depends on how willing the media is to accept that talking point," said Arthur, now at the Center for Immigration Studies. Arthur said DHS can largely proceed as usual with its previously established funding while any investigations take place, adding that much of what Mullin and Trump have done already falls under established law that Congress itself passed. Referencing the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, Arthur said that, short of "amending the law itself – which they can’t do if [Trump] vetoes it" Democrats can probe and try to paint the agency in a "bad light" over ICE-involved shootings and similar incidents, but that their larger agenda would be buttressed by the INA. articles.title: Postelection power struggle brewing
articles.summary: Plus: 😬 GOP reckons with midterm fallout {beacon} It’s Friday. At least the weekend always has bipartisan support. In today’s issue: Leadership shake-up on the horizon GOP searches for answers Stock market reaction Trump arch on hold Programming note: Hello! articles.body:
It’s Friday. At least the weekend always has bipartisan support.

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Jose Luis Magana, Mariam Zuhaib, J. Scott Applewhite and Jae C. Hong

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is the only party leader in Congress who isn’t facing opposition — or at least reservations — on their path to a leadership position.

DropSite is keeping a scorecard on where progressive lawmakers are lining up on Jeffries. It seems all but inevitable that he will be America’s first Black Speaker of the House, taking charge of a historic majority.

Not so in the races for House minority leader and Senate minority leader.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) seems on track to return to leading the majority, though he won’t be getting a unanimous vote. Incoming senators including Abdul El-Sayed (Mich.), Juliana Stratton (Ill.) and Adam Hamilton (Kan.) pledged to cast their vote for a new face atop the caucus.

It’s still unclear who might get their votes. El-Sayed said this week he’d support Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) for the role. Van Hollen’s office put out a statement Thursday saying he’s not interested.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is firmly in pole position after announcing his intention to remain GOP leader in the minority. In some of the biggest disappointments for Senate Republicans — including Georgia, Texas, South Carolina and North Carolina — President Trump hand-selected the GOP candidates, pushing out popular senators in two of those states.

That may help Thune argue he’s still the right man for the job of preparing for 2028.

No one has announced a run against him — yet.

Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz publicly called on Senate Republicans to look beyond Thune, accusing the party of “rewarding failure” after sweeping midterm losses.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is out , as usually happens to a Speaker who loses the chamber. Running to replace him are House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) — and maybe more.

The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi has all the deets and drama here .

There’s competition for other House GOP leadership roles, too.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is running against House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.). And GOP Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.) both intend to oppose House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (Mich.).

Wall Street celebrated Tuesday’s election results with a major rally Wednesday. But by Thursday, the party was over.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged more than 1,800 points , while the S&P 500 dropped 4.4 percent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite sank 5.5 percent. The sell-off wiped out Wednesday’s gains as investors grew nervous about the future of artificial intelligence and data center projects following Democrats’ midterm victories.

It marks another headache for Trump, who has repeatedly touted stock market gains as proof of his economic success.

The president cast blame on Democrats for the turmoil:

“Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this,” he wrote on Truth Social . “Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats.”

The job market still has some gas in the tank.

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, nearly tripling economists’ expectations of 59,000. The unemployment rate also ticked down to 4.1 percent, according to data released Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The agency also revised its August and September hiring numbers upward, giving the economic outlook another boost.

But don’t break out the champagne just yet. Wages grew 3.1 percent over the past year, trailing September’s 3.7 percent inflation rate.

In other words, Americans may be finding work, but their paychecks may not be stretching quite as far.

New York Federal Reserve President John Williams warned this week that inflation remains too high.

Annual inflation hit 3.7 percent in September, marking the seventh straight month above 3 percent. And with another interest rate hike potentially on the table in December, the nation’s central bank faces some tough decisions ahead.

➤ CAMPAIGN PROMISES TO CONGRESSIONAL PRESSURE:

Democrats rode frustration over soaring diesel and beef prices to victories in farm-heavy states on Tuesday.

Now comes the hard part: delivering relief to the farmers who helped put them in power.

From the Iran war to Trump’s tariffs, the incoming majority faces some tough choices — and a president who can veto its proposals.

👓 Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Max Rego.

Explore 2026 election results, voting trends and historical comparisons with Decision Desk HQ, available through The Hill Insider Premium.

A federal judge has thrown a wrench into Trump’s plans to build a triumphal arch between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, putting the brakes on the construction project — at least for two weeks.

The Thursday ruling from U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan came not long after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the proposal , following a contentious public meeting that was briefly disrupted by technology issues.

The arch has faced legal challenges and fierce opposition from critics — including officials in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — who argue the project threatens nearby historic landmarks

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) celebrated the ruling , calling the proposed arch a monument to Trump’s “own ego” and vowing to work with incoming Democratic majorities in Congress to stop it permanently.

Meanwhile: The president has another proposal . He wants to designate the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments, potentially limiting future presidents’ ability to renovate them — even as he continues his own White House makeover with the ongoing ballroom project and recently upgraded helipad .

🪖 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ’s future at the Pentagon is looking increasingly uncertain as some within the Trump administration blame him for the Iran war and the GOP’s midterm defeats. The president is reportedly asking allies about the Defense chief’s standing, though he continues to defend him publicly.

⚖️ Jason Reding Quiñones , the top federal prosecutor in South Florida, and John Eisenberg , assistant attorney general for the national security division, resigned Friday , marking more high-profile departures from the Justice Department. Their exits come a day after Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon stepped down .

🗳️ How did Generation Z help swing the midterms to the left? Young voters shifted sharply away from Trump after his gains with the demographic in 2024, with roughly two-thirds backing Democratic candidates in Tuesday’s elections. Read more in The Feed .

🔎 Impeachment talk is already brewing on Capitol Hill, with two House Democrats floating the idea of ousting Attorney General Todd Blanche . Meanwhile, Scalise is urging Republicans to prepare for an expected wave of Democratic investigations.
