articles.title: How Paraguay’s Ueno collapse is only its latest banking crisis
articles.summary: President Santiago Pena is under fire over links to parent company of collapsed bank.
articles.body:
Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital bank, which has plunged the South American country into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade.

Pena announced his resignation on Thursday, but politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president. Pena, a former International Monetary Fund (IMF) economist, then requested a 72-hour extension to present his defence at an impeachment hearing, because he had been given less than 12 hours to answer “an accusatory writ and about 300 pages of attachments”, adding: “That is not due process.”

However, the Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove him from office.

Until March 2025, Pena held a stake in Grupo Vazquez, the parent company that owns Ueno Bank.

Ueno Bank was established in 1976 and remained a small financial operation for decades.

After being granted a full banking licence in 2023, it rebranded and grew to become a household name in Paraguay within five years. Customers were incentivised with cashback offers on groceries and it built a network of more than 70 branches. The bank sponsored Paraguay’s national football team and its name was plastered across the country’s main stadium.

Ueno bank reported that it had 3 million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population.

The digital bank managed $800m of public funds, including about $380m invested by Paraguay’s state pension and health fund, according to data from the Central Bank of Paraguay.

On Monday, Paraguay’s central bank decided to put Ueno bank into resolution – the strongest action it can take short of placing the bank into liquidation – after finding that its solvency ratio, a measure of its capital against its risk-weighted assets, had dropped to less than half of the legal requirement.

Resolution allows regulators to transfer a failing bank’s deposits to other institutions before liquidating remaining assets.

Customer accounts were frozen, leaving millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their savings and unpaid wages.

Ueno Bank’s nearly 3 million customers still cannot withdraw cash, make digital payments or use their bank cards.

“Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder,” he added, an apparent reference to the right-wing Colorado Party which has ruled Paraguay almost uninterrupted for more than seven decades.

Regulators at Paraguay’s central bank found a pattern of risky lending to “insiders”, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. This means that executives or major investors of a bank have approved questionable, low-security loans for themselves, their families or their own businesses. In this case, Ueno had loaned $146m to companies tied to its owner, Grupo Vasquez, which has links to Paraguay’s president.

Investigators found loaned amounts went beyond legal limits and were not backed up by enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

Central Bank regulators found Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners were poorly documented while the bank had wrongly counted some expenses as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, was revealed to be less than half the legal minimum.

Protesters blame President Pena personally for the crisis because of his ties to the failed bank. Until recently, he held a financial stake in Ueno Bank’s parent holding company. After taking office in 2023, Pena appointed the former head of Ueno’s predecessor company, Carlos Carvallo, to head the country’s central bank, giving an insider the role of overseeing the institution. Carvallo has resigned from his position.

Pena denies any improper ties to the bank.

Protesters also say they are unhappy that so much public pension money was invested with the bank under Pena despite warnings about its high-risk insider lending practices.

What happens to people with savings in the bank now?

Paraguay’s Congress rushed through a law on Wednesday, providing a state-guaranteed fund for repaying depositors within five business days, starting on Thursday with small accounts holding up to $1,600.

The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 percent of customers.

Paraguay’s Public Prosector’s office has ordered multiple criminal investigations. On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, to be detained pending trial, while two others were placed under house arrest. In all, prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud.

Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena has tried to step down and wants Congress to approve his resignation. However, opposition politicians want him to be formally removed from office rather than merely allowing him to resign. They argue that allowing Pena to step down would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and shield him from possible prosecution.

Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolon Fernandez has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Pena and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor’s office said on Thursday.

The investigations will examine authorities’ oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.

Is this the first banking crisis in Paraguay?

No. Paraguay has a long history of bank failures and went through a prolonged banking crisis from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s.

In 1995, the central bank was forced to close Bancopar, which had severe liquidity problems and had also practised insider lending to companies linked to the bank’s owners. Three more banks also failed because of risky practices and poor oversight. The government was forced to cover the deposits of customers of all four banks, causing lasting damage to public confidence in Paraguay’s banking system.

Other banks including Banco General, and Banco Aleman were closed in this era. Banco Union and the state-linked Banco Nacional de Trabajadores and Banco Plus also failed.

Banco Espirito Santo in Portugal collapsed in 2014 with losses of $4.8bn when it was revealed that the family-controlled banking group had hidden losses. The Bank of Portugal had to split and rescue what was the country’s second largest private bank. That happened as Portugal was recovering from a deep recession, austerity cuts and bail-out obligations to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European Commission.

In 2008, the three major commercial banks in Iceland – Glitnir, Kaupthing and Landsbanki – all collapsed within days following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. The three banks were heavily exposed because they had borrowed from foreign capital markets far too aggressively. Iceland did not shore up the banks, instead seeking help from the IMF and launching criminal investigations.

The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered banking crises in other countries, including the United Kingdom, but banks there were mostly propped up or rescued by governments.

Fraud and insider lending caused the collapse of Banco Intercontinental Baninter in the Dominican Republic in 2003 with losses of $2.2bn.

And in 1991, Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a globally active bank, collapsed with losses of $10bn. Extensive fraud, hidden bad loans, and illicit operations masked the true scale of the deficit until the intervention of regulators. It was shut it down simultaneously in more than 70 countries.

articles.body:
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), the chair of the powerful House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, said Friday “there’s a lot of questions” in the Republican conference about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) prepares for an impeachment push next week.

“Well, that’s going to be a decision that President Trump’s going to have to make,” Comer said during his appearance on The Hill’s partner network NewsNation when asked if he wants a new face in the Pentagon.

“But I can tell you with a high level of confidence that … there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

Comer’s comments come as The Hill reported that Trump has been asking allies about Hegseth’s standing, and one of the sources said the Pentagon chief is in “a lot of trouble.”

Publicly, Trump has defended Hegseth, saying he was not considering replacing the Defense secretary and that Hegseth, a former Army National Guard major, is “doing a very good job.”

A senior Pentagon official told The Hill on Thursday the prospect of Hegseth being replaced is not “practical,” noting the difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck session — and before Democrats take control of the House following the midterm blue tsunami .

“He is not terribly worried about being replaced,” the senior Pentagon official said.

Hegseth is also expected to face an impeachment salvo in the lame-duck session from Massie, who said he would reintroduce articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief.

The Defense secretary ripped the impeachment push as nothing more than political theater from a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.”

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in a video posted Thursday. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Massie, a vocal critic of the Iran war, has said he would not reintroduce the resolution, which is expected to have significant support from Democrats and some Republicans, if Hegseth resigns.

Comer also said Friday he has heard from Republican voters who are “mad” about the Iran war, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and are dissatisfied with the rise in gas prices.

“They are mad that we’re in this situation in Iran,” Comer told NewsNation host Markie Martin. “They’re mad over gas prices, and a lot of them stayed home. I do not think, at least in Kentucky, I don’t think that these upset MAGA people voted Democrat. They just didn’t vote. So we’ve got to regain their trust. I think we can do it.”

articles.title: Bannon says Susie Wiles should be ‘removed immediately’
articles.summary: Former White House adviser Steve Bannon said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and other political consultants should be “removed immediately” following the losses suffered by the GOP in the midterm elections. Democrats secured wins in battleground states across the country on Tuesday, flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Ohio,…
articles.body:
Former White House adviser Steve Bannon said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and other political consultants should be “removed immediately” following the losses suffered by the GOP in the midterm elections.

Democrats secured wins in battleground states across the country on Tuesday, flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Ohio, among others.

“I think that you have to look to people like Susie Wiles, the chief of staff, and the political consultants that are there … because of the results, they should be removed and removed immediately,” Bannon said in an interview with British journalist Steven Edginton.

Bannon is not the first to call for Wiles’s removal.

On Wednesday, Caroline Sunshine, a former staffer to President Trump, told Fox News that Wiles “ needs to resign ” and “offer her resignation to the president before he has to ask for it. Her campaign skills have not translated into governing.”

Bannon, in his interview, also raised concerns over Texas turning blue in the midterm elections.

In the Lone Star State, where Republicans have historically maintained a stronghold for years, Democratic candidates emerged victorious in key races. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott to be elected as the state’s first Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1994.

Democrat James Talarico also defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) to become the first Democratic senator from the state since 1988.

“Right now, in Texas we have a fight,” Bannon said, adding that the new governor “can make Texas a sanctuary state.”

“If Texas is a sanctuary state like New York and California, you’re seeing the end of this republic as you know it,” he added.

Talarico, in a recent interview with Forbes , said he is willing to work with the Trump administration on immigration.

“I think there is an opportunity here to finally pass comprehensive immigration reform, to secure our border,” he said. “And also create more legal pathways for hard-working immigrants to come to this country, contribute to this economy and make us richer and stronger as a nation.”

articles.title: Jon Stewart flames Chuck Schumer; Dems must get ready to govern
articles.summary: Democrats need to be careful — they cannot spend the next two years proving they are better at fighting Republicans than they are at improving people’s lives.
articles.body:
John Stewart has a plan for the Dems when they re-take office in January.

“Job one of this opportunity is to tear down the obstacles and old way of thinking that got us into this mess,” Said the “Daily Show” comedian. “Someone has to meet this moment and they have got to show — and this moment is not, ‘oh, we get to impeach everybody’ … like, you have an opportunity to actually govern.”

Democrats just secured some major political victories. But winning an election and keeping the trust of voters are two very different things. Democrats would be making a mistake if they assumed this victory automatically validates the congressional leadership that got them here. It does not.

On his podcast, “The Weekly Show,” Stewart went a step further, taking aim at Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer:

“By the way, they’re already like, ‘Chuck Schumer deserves a lot of credit’ … Chuck Schumer fought tooth and nail against half of these [BLEEP] people! And even if he didn’t, he does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands. I truly believe that.”

He went on to say that many senior leaders need to go, and folks should remember Schumer was the genius that brought us Haley Stevens. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, was the genius who previously co-sponsored Medicare for All legislation and then went on national TV and said he’s changed his mind.

Schumer and Jeffries were also congratulated by AIPAC on their wins this week.

“AIPAC congratulates the hundreds of pro-Israel Democrats and Republicans who won their elections last night. More than 234 candidates supported by AIPAC members have already won, with many additional races still too close to call. We congratulate Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries on the resounding victories for their caucuses.”

Meanwhile, both Schumer and Jeffries have faced criticism from progressives over their relationship with AIPAC and their reluctance to embrace candidates like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and others.

The political landscape surrounding AIPAC is changing. Even Republicans are questioning our countries ties to Israel. The group and affiliated organizations spent nearly $30 million backing Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, an enormous investment that ultimately did not prevent progressive challenger Abdul El-Sayed from winning the nomination. Then the group poured money into Mike Rogers campaign. El-Sayed still won the entire election.

But I digress. Democrats need to be careful — they cannot spend the next two years proving they are better at fighting Republicans than they are at improving people’s lives.

Yes, there should be accountability, investigations and credible abuses of power should be examined. For example, Democrats should investigate the reported interference with Ukraine’s access to Musk’s Starlink and Starshield systems, as well as the financial relationships surrounding President Trump’s family crypto ventures, including Binance’s role in facilitating his family’s stablecoin and Trump’s subsequent pardon of the Binance founder.

But hear me clearly: making impeachment the centerpiece of the new majority’s agenda would be a mistake.

I say that as someone deeply critical of Trump and his administration. Do not let governing fall to the wayside. People are seriously struggling out here. A recent AP Voter Poll found that 79 percent of voters said inflation had caused their households either moderate or severe financial hardship. That’s the reality Democrats need to confront. Groceries, housing, health care, utilities. These are not abstract political talking points. This is serious.

Schumer does not automatically have to become Senate majority leader, and Jeffries does not automatically have to become Speaker of the House. Those positions require support from their respective caucuses. Neither of them have an entitlement to the job.

This could be an opportunity to look beyond the familiar names and find new leaders, with fewer big-pocket donors, who are willing to speak to working families, connect with younger voters, challenge entrenched political interests and offer something more compelling than simply being the alternative to Donald Trump.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

The leadership PAC, a committee not connected to his campaign and meant to raise money for his political allies, is the latest sign that El-Sayed aims to…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) has launched Habibi PAC, his own political action committee, just days after punching his ticket to the upper chamber, Federal Election Commission filings show.

The leadership PAC, a committee not connected to his campaign and meant to raise money for his political allies, is the latest sign that El-Sayed aims to influence Democratic politics into the future. El-Sayed has used the word Habibi , an Arabic term of endearment meaning “my beloved” but often used more casually, to address his opponents in the wake of Tuesday’s win.

“JD, habibi,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech, addressing Vice President Vance who has harshly criticized the Michigander. “There is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”

Arabic terminology and culture were present throughout the El-Sayed campaign as he pushed to become the first Muslim U.S. senator. Supporters often wore “Habibi for Abdul” shirts on the campaign trail.

El-Sayed won by a wide margin Tuesday in a key swing state for the 2028 presidential election, potentially positioning him to influence the likely expansive Democratic primary field of candidates as they make their way through the Midwest state.

El-Sayed ran as an unapologetic Muslim with strong views against sending military aid to Israel. Facing incessant attacks over his religion, El-Sayed aired an ad emphasizing his faith and his mission “to serve God and to serve our neighbors.”

President Trump has often called El-Sayed a “jihadist” and purposefully misstated his name — calling him by his middle name, Mohamed. Former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), the Republican candidate, often attempted to tie him to extremist organizations to which El-Sayed has no connection.

The newest Michigan senator used the playful nickname of Habibi to push back on the right-wing rhetoric about his religion, and he has now employed the phrase in his effort to raise money for future political allies.

articles.title: Trump backs Gruters’s reelection bid as RNC chair
articles.summary: President Trump formally backed Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters’s reelection bid on Friday following the party’s widespread losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. “Joe Gruters should return as Chairman of the RNC to continue to build our Party, and be a trusted partner as we MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, and ensure Free and Fair…
articles.body:
President Trump formally backed Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters’s reelection bid on Friday following the party’s widespread losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“Joe Gruters should return as Chairman of the RNC to continue to build our Party, and be a trusted partner as we MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, and ensure Free and Fair Elections. Republicans everywhere should support him as he continues his mission at the RNC,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

The president called Gruters “100 [percent] America First,” and noted the party’s grassroots love him.

“As Chairman, Joe turned the RNC into an efficient, focused, and powerful machine that will continue to empower the America First Agenda for many years to come,” he said.

Trump’s endorsement comes after RNC co-Chair KC Crosbie, another Trump ally, announced she would challenge Gruters for his role in January.

“Tuesday’s results were a serious setback. Democrats will control both chambers of Congress, and we lost in places we have long counted on,” Crosbie wrote in a letter announcing her challenge to Gruters. “We owe ourselves an honest account of why. Voters were focused on the cost of living, and the direction of the country. Our improvements in field operations, voter contact, and election integrity infrastructure were valuable, but they did not address those concerns or deliver the results we needed.”

Democrats scored widespread victories in the midterm elections, winning key battleground states, flipping a number of red states and gaining majorities in state legislatures.

Democrats hold a 54-44 majority in the Senate as of Friday, and they led 253-158 for seats in the House, according to The Hill’s partner DDHQ.

articles.title: Susie Wiles out, Stephen Miller in, as Trump’s chief of staff
articles.summary: President Trump announced Friday that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is leaving the White House and longtime adviser Stephen Miller will take her place. The move comes after Republicans suffered sweeping defeats in the midterms, losing dozens of House seats and control of the Senate. “I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller,…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Friday that his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is leaving the White House and longtime adviser Stephen Miller will take her place.

The move comes after Republicans suffered sweeping defeats in the midterms, losing dozens of House seats and control of the Senate.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

A White House official said Wiles gave her resignation on Thursday night.

When leaving the White House after the announcement, Trump told reporters, “we’ve got to make some moves.”

Questions have swirled over whether there will be shake-ups in the White House staff since the blue wave proved very real Tuesday.

Former White House adviser Steve Bannon said Friday that Wiles should be “ removed immediately ” over the GOP’s loss.

“I think that you have to look to people like Susie Wiles, the chief of staff, and the political consultants that are there … because of the results, they should be removed and removed immediately,” Bannon said in an interview with British journalist Steven Edginton.

Former Trump staffer Caroline Sunshine also called for Wiles to resign Wednesday over the losses.

“Susie Wiles needs to resign,” she told Fox News’s Jesse Watters. “She needs to offer her resignation to the president before he has to ask for it. Her campaign skills have not translated into governing. Susie was behind the historic win in 2024, and she deserved credit for it and got the top job for it.”

Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney told NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” that he expects Wiles to leave the position after the midterms.

“It’s just a natural sort of time to make that change,” he said.

Wiles said in a post on social platform X that Friday would be her last day in the job.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” she wrote.

“More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

Congratulatory messages started rolling in for Miller, who has been in Trump’s circle since 2016 when he left his job as a congressional aide to U.S. Sen. Jeff Sessions (R-Ala.) to be Trump’s senior policy advisor for his first presidential campaign.

Vice President Vance said he was “very grateful to Susie for her friendship and service to the president and our country.”

“Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things. Congrats to him on a well-deserved promotion!” he wrote.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote “huge CONGRATS” to Miller on X, calling him a true patriot and American First fighter.”

“He never backs down — and the @DeptofWar is right there with him,” he wrote.

Hegseth’s position has also been questioned following the midterms as several officials have placed the blame of the loss on the unpopularity of the Iran war.

Bill Pulte, director of U.S. federal housing and former acting director of national intelligence, also shared his congratulations and said , “I can’t wait to work with you.”

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt called Wiles “one of the kindest and toughest people I’ve ever met.”

“She helped power the greatest political comeback in American history in 2024, and as the first woman to serve as White House Chief of Staff, she led the most productive start to a presidency in decades, even while battling breast cancer,” she wrote. “I’m proud to call her my friend and former boss.”

She said Trump “made the perfect choice” in choosing Miller, who “will make the final two years of the President’s term a resounding success.”

However, Democrats were quick to decry the pick.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) wrote that Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” he wrote . “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, said, “The American people are begging the White House to focus on lowering costs, but the best Trump can do is ‘more Stephen Miller and the culture of cruelty.’”

articles.title: Giuliani says Vance as president could be a ‘dangerous possibility’
articles.summary: Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani (R) on Thursday said he sees “presidential potential” in Vice President Vance but raised concerns about “certain dangers” in his personality. “I see presidential potential with you,” Giuliani said, directly addressing Vance during a livestream on his YouTube channel. “I also see certain dangers in your personality, which…
articles.body:
Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani (R) on Thursday said he sees “presidential potential” in Vice President Vance but raised concerns about “certain dangers” in his personality.

“I see presidential potential with you,” Giuliani said, directly addressing Vance during a livestream on his YouTube channel. “I also see certain dangers in your personality, which make you a dangerous possibility as president.”

“To be president, you have to have the flexibility of mind, not to have slogans dominate your thinking,” Giuliani said in response to Vance’s remarks following the midterm results. “That’s the feeling I got from you yesterday when you said that the election was determined by the war.”

He added “it wasn’t mainly, mostly determined by the war. The war was a sub part.”

Vance in a lengthy post online on Wednesday pinned the blame for the GOP’s losses of the House and Senate majorities on the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

The ongoing Middle East conflict was a concern for voters leading up to Election Day. In a recent Gallup poll , released before the midterms, roughly 47 percent of voters said the war would be an “extremely” important issue when casting their vote while 30 percent said it would be “very” important.

Giuliani said it was the “economy” that was the deciding factor in the elections. The same Gallup survey found half of the respondents marked the economy as an extremely important factor in casting their ballots.

Vance, who has faced criticism from some on the right for his Wednesday statement, is seen as the front-runner for the GOP White House nomination in 2028. Many observers also think his presidential aspirations have taken a hit from the midterm defeats, which were seen as a repudiation of the Trump White House.

Last month, the vice president said if he runs for president in 2028, President Trump would endorse him . Asked about those comments, Trump did not say if he would endorse Vance , noting, “I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” before adding “he’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person.”

articles.title: Democrats flip battleground Michigan House seat, ousting Huizenga
articles.summary: Democrat Sean McCann has won Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, ousting longtime Rep. Bill Huizenga (R), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Huizenga h...
articles.body:
Democrat Sean McCann has won Michigan's 4th Congressional District, ousting longtime Rep. Bill Huizenga (R), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Huizenga has represented western Michigan in the House for more than a decade. While he easily won his last race in 2024, the district has become more competitive in recent years and was viewed as a key pickup opportunity for Democrats this year.

McCann, a member of the Michigan state Senate, was tapped to be part of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's "Red to Blue" program, which aimed to flip Republican-held seats.

He also received support from prominent Michigan Democrats, including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

McCann defeated Huizenga by 1.81 percentage points, DDHQ reports.

Huizenga, a key player on the House Financial Services Committee, initially weighed a run for Senate last year before seeking reelection in his southwestern Michigan district.

He ultimately decided against a bid for retiring Sen. Gary Peters's (D) seat, clearing the way for former Rep. Mike Rogers to run as the Republican nominee.

articles.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
articles.summary: Susie Wiles steps down as White House chief of staff; Stephen Miller assumes the role amid post-election reshuffling.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has announced that Stephen Miller is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

In a post on his Truth Social account on Friday, Trump said Miller would start his new job on Monday, calling him “one of my most trusted advisors”.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

Wiles, the most high-profile departure yet from the White House after Republicans’ overwhelming midterm losses, said Friday would be her last day.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honour of a lifetime”, she wrote in a social media post. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First”.

Al Jazeera learned that Wiles, who oversaw Trump’s return to the presidency in 2024, handed her resignation to Trump in the White House’s Oval Office on Thursday. A Republican Party official confirmed it was accepted by the president, who has since said he wanted to make a change.

Miller has been one of Trump’s closest confidants throughout both presidential terms, after joining the president’s first election campaign as an adviser in 2016.

Democrats are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller upon taking control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the likely incoming chairman of the US House’s Oversight Committee, said in a statement to Al Jazeera. “Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts.”

He added, “Stephen Miller should lawyer up”.

Trump was widely expected to shake up his staff after the midterm drubbing, which saw Democrats net seven US Senate seats, with two states, Alaska and Mississippi, still counting their results. Democrats, as of Friday, have also won 253 seats in the 435-member US House, with 27 races still set to be counted.

Despite the vote, which was widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, Miller’s appointment largely represents a doubling down on his most controversial policies, offering a potential view of the course the president plans to chart for his final two years in office.

Miller, a domestic adviser to the president, has been the driving force behind some of the Trump administration’s most controversial policies, including its far-reaching immigration crackdown in the US.

Garcia called Miller “the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorised our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families”.

Some White House staff members immediately praised the announcement soon after it was announced.

“Stephen Miller is a Trump OG, someone who has been with the President since the very beginning”, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on X. “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen, and he will help the Administration deliver on monumental victories for the rest of this historic second term”.

Miller has not yet commented on the election results, but on election day, he urged Trump supporters to vote in a post on X.

“Send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future and destroy the inheritance of your children,” he wrote. “Get to the polls and protect the ones you love.”

articles.title: Carney welcomes Democrats' push to end Trump's tariffs on Canada after midterm victory
articles.summary: TORONTO (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed a Democratic push to repeal U. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canada after their sweeping mi...
articles.body:
TORONTO (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed a Democratic push to repeal U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada after their sweeping midterm victory, saying Friday that restoring free trade would lower costs for American families and benefit U.S. workers, even as Ottawa continues negotiating with Washington.

"We welcome any moves to restore a free trading arrangement between Canada and the United States, which is in the interests of American families struggling with affordability," Carney told reporters in Winnipeg.

He said free trade would also benefit American workers seeking well-paying jobs and stability.

"We will continue to work with the Americans to get a deal that works for Canada," Carney said.

The Democratic victory raises a dilemma for Canada: Accept a deal that reduces Trump's tariffs but leaves some in place, or hold out for the restoration of free trade as the incoming Congress prepares to challenge them. Carney has not said whether the election has changed his negotiating position .

Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, who is poised to chair the Senate Finance Committee when Democrats take control of Congress in January, has identified Trump's tariffs on Canada as an early target for repeal.

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat, said Thursday he was willing to work with Trump on "stopping these stupid tariffs with Canada."

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer introduced legislation in September aimed at repealing Trump's tariffs, including duties imposed on Canadian goods.

Carney said he had not spoken with Wyden or other Democrats about potential legislation to eliminate the tariffs.

Trump retains broad authority over trade policy and could veto legislation repealing the tariffs. Democrats would need substantial Republican support to override a veto.

Canada suspended trade talks in August over U.S. demands that Carney said threatened Canadian sovereignty and French-language protections. Trump's trade war has included 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.

Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st U.S. state and has pushed to move Canadian automobile production to the United States.

Trump has also threatened new tariffs on Canadian automobiles beginning in January, adding pressure on Canada's auto industry as Ottawa weighs whether to strike a deal now or hold out for the elimination of U.S. tariffs.

Relations have improved in recent weeks. Trump said Sunday the countries were "very close" to an agreement, while Carney said Tuesday that Washington had backed away from demands involving Canada's French-language protections, culture and ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries.

articles.title: Jon Stewart says Schumer doesn’t understand ‘urgency of the moment’
articles.summary: Schumer indicated he has the votes to remain the Democratic leader, despite growing calls for a change at the top.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Comedian Jon Stewart, 63, says Democrats should use their midterm victories to move past the establishment and focus on governing.

With Democrats now controlling both chambers of Congress, Stewart said on Thursday’s episode of “The Weekly Show” podcast that “Job one of this opportunity is to tear down the obstacles and old way of thinking that got us into this mess.”

“The Daily Show” host added this involves removing the “system of seniority from Democratic politics,” partially in reference to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Stewart said Schumer “fought tooth and nail” against many of the Democratic candidates elected in the midterms and doesn’t deserve credit for their wins.

“And even if he didn’t, he does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands. I truly believe that,” he added.

This comes as Schumer, 75, recently indicated he has the votes to remain the Democratic leader, despite growing calls from some progressives for a change at the top .

The comedian added that Democrats should focus on actually governing, rather than trying to “impeach everybody” in the Trump administration, as some anticipate will happen .

“Someone has to meet this moment and they have got to show — and this moment is not, ‘Oh, we get to impeach everybody,’ like f— that. Like, you have an opportunity to actually govern. Do it. Take it,” Stewart said.

articles.body:
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) obtained the five signatures he needs from GOP colleagues to request a meeting of the broader Senate Republican Conference to discuss postponing their leadership election, which is scheduled for next week.

Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, is seeking a delay of the election after an adviser of President Trump questioned whether Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) should be reelected to lead the caucus, according to a Senate GOP aide familiar with the effort.

No senator, however, has publicly expressed an interest in challenging Thune, who remains popular among his GOP colleagues in the upper chamber. The group raised more than $800 million to protect the Senate Republican majority in this election cycle.

The conference rules provide for Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, to call a meeting of the group whenever requested to do so in writing by five or more colleagues.

The Senate Republican Conference is already scheduled to meet Tuesday morning to vote on its new leadership team.

Johnson’s letter requesting a pause on that timeline is a signal to colleagues that he wants to discuss postponing the vote before colleagues fill out their secret ballots on reelecting Thune and other members of his leadership team.

Senate conservatives also sought to delay their conference’s leadership contest after the 2024 election, when Republicans picked up four Democratic-held seats and captured the majority. That effort wasn’t successful.

Alex Bruesewitz called for Senate Republicans to find new leaders in the wake of Republicans’ losses across the country earlier this week, which will cost them control of at least seven seats in next year’s Congress.

“I saw a report that says Senator John Thune is gliding into the Senate Minority Leader role,” Bruesewitz posted on the social platform X. “Why do Hill Republicans insist on rewarding failure?”

He added, “He’s not exactly in touch with the interests of Republican voters. Perhaps it’s time to give someone else a chance?”

articles.body:
Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said in a statement Friday that he was discharged from the Johns Hopkins Hospital and will spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center as he recovers from a stroke.

Murphy will miss “the next several weeks of votes” as he continues his recovery. The senator said he was diagnosed with a “small” stroke after feeling unwell last Saturday, and his office announced the medical emergency in a statement one day after it occurred.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far,” Murphy said in the statement.

The Connecticut Democrat is seen as a rising star in his party and has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender.

Members of Congress are not required to disclose medical events that affect their ability to participate in official business, and many keep details from the public until after they recover. Murphy joins at least two other Democratic senators who have disclosed a stroke in recent memory — Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.).

“This has been a scary experience for me and my family, and I appreciate the continued respect for our privacy,” Murphy said. “As I’m working towards a full recovery, I am staying engaged with my team and colleagues remotely, and my staff continues to carry out our legislative priorities, serve constituents, and ensure the work of my office continues uninterrupted.”

Murphy thanked the doctors and staff at Johns Hopkins for their treatment and care for his family. Jose Suarez, chief of neurosciences critical care at the Johns Hopkins Hospital, is quoted in the statement saying Murphy will make a full recovery.

“Senator Murphy experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke. He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation,” Suarez said.

articles.title: Christie mulling White House bid, says ‘Trump era is over’
articles.summary: Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) is considering a White House run in 2028, telling his party to go in “a completely different direction” after sizable midterm losses. In an interview with Politico on Wednesday, Christie said he sees himself as better positioned to run than other prominent Republicans — specifically Vice President Vance…
articles.body:
Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie (R) is considering a White House run in 2028, telling his party to go in “a completely different direction” after sizable midterm losses.

In an interview with Politico on Wednesday, Christie said he sees himself as better positioned to run than other prominent Republicans — specifically Vice President Vance — because he has consistently criticized President Trump during his second term. He called out Vance’s post blaming GOP losses on the Iran war, which Vance has publicly supported.

“The vice president to me has no credibility. He’s been sitting in the White House now for the last two years,” Christie told Politico. “[I] haven’t heard him say a negative word, you know, until this past Wednesday, and he limited it just to the war in Iran, which is not the only problem we have here.”

The two-time presidential candidate may launch a third campaign in 2028, he told Politico, saying he would make that decision “in the next few months.”

During his 2024 campaign , Christie urged the party to move on from Trump rather than nominate him again and was one of the only candidates who was willing to take on the president directly.

“The Trump era is over,” he told Politico. “We need to look forward to new leadership in our party and our country.”

After ending his campaign, Christie did not endorse a 2024 candidate.

Major midterm losses for the GOP, coupled with the president’s unpopularity, could mean that the party chooses to pivot away from Trump in the 2028 presidential primaries.

Jockeying is already underway for those primaries. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), usually a Trump ally, called the midterms a “rebuke” of the president.

Christie also singled out DeSantis in his Politico interview, accusing him of seeking “a way to be relevant.”

“I think the governor is getting ready to leave office, and he’s looking for a way to be relevant,” Christie said. “And I think he looks like he’s talking out of both sides of his mouth.”

Other Republicans releasing election postmortems include Texas Sens. Ted Cruz and John Cornyn, who criticized their party and encouraged it to focus more on cost-of-living issues. Cruz and Cornyn’s home state was the site of major political upsets Tuesday as Democrats swept the statewide races. Cruz, also a previous presidential candidate, is considered a possible contender in 2028.

Candidates for the next presidential election could announce bids in the coming weeks or months. In 2022, Trump announced he would run again right after the midterms .

articles.title: South Florida candidate sues election official, alleging bias in a contentious, razor-thin race
articles.summary: MIAMI — South Florida Democratic congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez filed a federal lawsuit against the Miami-Dade supervisor of elections Friday, citing bias after she declined to recuse herself from the recount process.
articles.body: MIAMI — South Florida Democratic congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez filed a federal lawsuit against the Miami-Dade supervisor of elections Friday, citing bias after she declined to recuse herself from the recount process. Incumbent Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar is named in the lawsuit as well. The lawsuit seeks to bar Miami-Dade supervisor of elections, Alina García, from acting as a deciding member of the county canvassing board for the 27th Congressional District, where the results are razor-thin. Salazar was leading Rodriguez by 1,103 votes or 0.44 percentage points as of Thursday evening. Florida law requires automatic recounts when there is less than a 0.5-point margin. The canvassing board oversees the recount. Rodriguez’s campaign demanded Thursday that García recuse herself from oversight of the recount. The Rodriguez campaign alleged the attorney representing Salazar in the recount, Robert Fernández, is García’s son-in-law and requested immediate confirmation, saying the relationship would raise additional serious concerns, according to the complaint. The campaign also cited in the lawsuit an interview García gave to The Miami Herald on election night stating, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount” and that it was “possible but not probable” there were enough remaining ballots to flip the results. She added that recounts almost never end up going the other way. “Usually the trend we see is what continues,” García was quoted as saying. In other words, if Salazar is ahead, it will likely remain that way. The Miami Herald also reported that Oren Rosenthal, general counsel for the supervisor of elections, estimated he’s seen about 20 recounts, and with the margin that Salazar was leading by on Tuesday night, he said it was unlikely the result will be overturned. The deputy supervisor of elections, Juan Mendieta, told NBC News, “There is no conflict. She is not recusing herself.” Juan-Carlos Planas, general counsel for the Miami-Dade Democratic Executive Committee, ran against García in the 2024 supervisor of elections race. “If candidates are going to hire relatives from the supervisor of elections, we’re going down a very dangerous precedent,” he said. “Can you imagine going into court and litigants are hiring relatives of the judge? The judge would be removed from office.” On Thursday evening, the day before the final counting of ballots and certification of results was scheduled to take place, an attorney representing Rodriguez sent a letter to García demanding she step away from matters involving the race. “This goes beyond any ethical standards. The canvassing board is a quasi-judicial body so she sits as a quasi-judicial official,” Planas said. “This is a quasi-judicial body and therefore she should recuse herself like any other judge would.” García, a Republican who served one term in the Florida state House before winning the election for supervisor of elections in 2024, has posed in pictures with fellow Republican leaders, including Salazar and President Donald Trump. She is the first elected supervisor of elections. It was previously a nonpartisan position appointed by the county’s mayor. Few pundits considered the race competitive this time around, but the district shifted 14.26 points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election. Salazar’s office did not respond to a request for comment. “My opponent is behaving like an election denier, attempting to turn this process into a political circus because he does not like election outcome,” Salazar posted on X Thursday night. Salazar and Rodriguez are both Cuban American and former journalists. Salazár has won three consecutive terms to represent the heavily Hispanic 27th Congressional District. She and Trump comfortably won the district in 2024. There were signs of trouble for Salazar in September when she released an ad where she broke with Trump on his immigration policies. “Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said in the ad while standing in front of the White House. Her district has been particularly impacted by Trump’s harsh immigration enforcement, including a record number of deportations of Cubans. While Trump criticized Salazar after the ad, he eventually endorsed her before Election Day.

articles.title: Jeffries calls Miller a ‘dangerous xenophobe’ after promotion: ‘Fire him today’
articles.summary: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is sounding off on Stephen Miller, President Trump’s pick to replace outgoing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a post to the social platform X. “His presence in government should…
articles.body:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is sounding off on Stephen Miller, President Trump’s pick to replace outgoing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries said in a post to the social platform X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Miller’s promotion is not likely to be well-received by Democrats, who view the new chief of staff as inflammatory and a hardliner. Miller is a primary architect of Trump’s strict immigration enforcement agenda, having pushed some of the president’s tougher policies over the years.

Last year, Miller said the Trump administration would seek to triple its daily immigration arrests to 3,000. He said the administration was actively looking into suspending habeas corpus rights, which allow those in custody to challenge their detention. And after two American citizens were shot and killed in Minneapolis by federal immigration agents, Miller referred to the victims as domestic terrorists .

Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, is one of several Democrats who blasted the move Friday. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump had “learned nothing” from the results of the midterms, in which Democrats stormed back into control of both chambers of Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, said Democrats would “continue to investigate” Miller.

“Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct,” Garcia said in a statement posted to X. “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Trump elevated Miller to the chief of staff role Friday, announcing in a post to Truth Social that Wiles would be leaving the role, just days after calling a report that Wiles may depart “TOTAL FAKE NEWS.”

Since Republicans’ midterm losses, some in the party, including former Trump adviser Steve Bannon, said Wiles should be fired . One former Trump aide, however, previously called the idea of Miller being chief of staff “terrifying.”

“The idea that in the last two years of Trump’s administration, when he’s going to be spiraling because he’s a lame-duck president,” former Deputy Press Secretary Sarah Matthews told MeidasTouch . “The idea of someone like a Stephen Miller in charge is a very scary thing.”

articles.title: Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
articles.summary: Miller has been a close confidant of Trump since 2016 and an architect of the president’s hardline immigration policies.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has tapped his longtime adviser Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff.

The move on Friday represented a doubling down on Trump’s most controversial policies following his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing earlier this week.

Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January, and are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller’s role in the White House.

The 41-year-old Miller has been one of Trump’s most vocal defenders and is widely seen as an architect of the president’s mass deportation campaign.

In his post on Truth Social, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors”, saying he would take over the role from Susie Wiles on Monday.

Miller had built a reputation as a conservative activist long before entering Trump’s orbit.

At Santa Monica High School, he cut his teeth railing against what he described as liberal school policies on local radio shows.

At Duke University, he led the Duke Conservative Union and became a staunch advocate for three of the school’s lacrosse players after they were accused of rape.

After college, he moved to Washington, DC, where he worked as a legislative aide to Republican members of Congress and Republican Senator Jeff Sessions.

He joined Trump’s initial presidential campaign in January 2016, where he was credited with shaping the president’s messaging and caustic political stylings.

“I think he and Trump hit it off from the very beginning,” former Trump adviser Steve Bannon told The Associated Press news agency in 2017. “I think he helped Trump find his voice.”

What was his role during Trump’s first term?

Following Trump’s surprise victory in the 2016 race, Miller assumed the role of presidential adviser and speechwriter.

He served as an influential voice in shaping Trump’s most strident actions related to immigration, often framing the issues as an effort to protect Western “civilisation”.

During that period, Democratic lawmakers accused Miller of perpetuating white nationalist rhetoric. In 2019, the Southern Poverty Law Center released emails allegedly showing the Trump adviser supporting white nationalist websites and ideologies.

He is credited with shaping the Department of Justice’s 2018 “Zero Tolerance” policy at the US border, which called for the arrest of nearly every adult crossing into the US without legal documentation.

The scheme resulted in widespread family separation , with children barred from being housed in criminal detention facilities along with their parents. Trump later changed the policy via executive order, amid widespread outrage.

As an adviser to Trump, Miller campaigned to end Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals ( DACA ), a programme that allowed individuals brought to the US as children without documentation to receive legal paperwork for education and employment. The programme stopped accepting new applicants in 2021.

Miller also drove wide-scale visa restrictions during Trump’s first term, including a 2017 travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, which came to be known as the “Muslim travel ban”.

The initial order blocked citizens of Syria, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen from entering the US for 90 days. An adjusted version of the policy was eventually upheld by the US Supreme Court.

He later became a top proponent of Trump’s unfounded claims that the 2020 election was stolen, supporting a scheme for Trump to be certified as the victor.

Miller remained by Trump’s side as the former president staged a political comeback ahead of the 2024 presidential vote. He became Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser when the administration retook office in January 2025.

Since then, he has helped to orchestrate Trump’s mass deportation drive, which has seen immigration enforcement agents flood communities across the country, increasingly targeting individuals with no or only minor criminal records.

In May 2025, Miller told Fox News the administration had “set a goal of a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day, and President Trump is going to keep pushing to get that number up higher each and every day”.

He has also been a vocal defender of increasingly violent tactics by immigration agents. He initially defended the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January. He initially called both Good and Pretti “terrorists” before walking back the statement about Pretti.

In his return to the White House, Miller also unsuccessfully sought to end birthright citizenship, while becoming an increasingly vocal defender of Trump’s military actions in the Western Hemisphere.

He endorsed the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and told CNN in January that the US had a right to seize Greenland based on its military might.

“We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said.

“These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”

It was not immediately clear how Miller’s new role would affect his influence over Trump.

The chief of staff is typically tasked with overseeing White House staff and hiring, maintaining the president’s calendar, and advising the president on policy.

Some insiders refer to the role, which largely controls information flows, as the “gatekeeper” to the presidency.
